en: A monastery on a bare limestone peak about 690 m above the Kornos plain, by tradition founded by Saint Helena around 327 to 329 CE and named for the relic of the True Cross she is said to have left there. It was one of the great pilgrimage stops of the crusader centuries and appears in the accounts of nearly every western traveller to Cyprus, who called it Santa Croce or the Mountain of the Holy Cross. Sacked in the medieval and early Ottoman centuries and gutted by fire in 1888, the present buildings are late, but the site itself and its relic are the oldest continuous Christian tradition on the island. Since 1889 it has kept Athonite rule, and women may not enter.

en: The best-preserved Gothic monastery in the eastern Mediterranean, founded between 1198 and 1205 by King Aimery for Augustinian canons who had fled Jerusalem after 1187 and handed to the Premonstratensian White Canons in 1206. The church went up under Hugh III (1267 to 1284) and the cloister and refectory under Hugh IV (1324 to 1359), who kept apartments here. The Genoese stripped it of everything portable in 1373, discipline had collapsed by 1489, and the Ottomans expelled the canons in 1571 and gave the buildings to the Orthodox Church. Its ruin above the coastal plain became the set piece of Lawrence Durrell's 'Bitter Lemons'.

en: A single-cell vaulted chapel barely 10 m long, the only surviving royal chapel of Frankish Cyprus, known locally as the Chapelle Royale. Tradition, following a lost inscription, credits it to King Janus in 1421 and shows him with his second wife Charlotte de Bourbon; a 2019 study of the style, iconography and lettering argues instead for the mid-fourteenth century and for Peter I and Eleanor of Aragon as the patrons. Either way it is a Latin building painted by a Greek-trained hand, with French, Cypriot, Armenian and Bourbon arms on the vault, and it shows how thoroughly the two traditions had mixed by the end of Lusignan rule.

en: Twin villages on the Yialias river that formed part of the Lusignan royal domain, and the best place to see how the crown actually made its money. Leontios Machairas records that Peter II built a country house at Potamia on the right bank of the river; King Janus camped his army here in 1426 before marching against the Mamluks, who burned the village the same year. Since 2000 a French mission with the University of Cyprus has surveyed and excavated the manor and the estate's wells, water-wheels, channels and mills. Two kilometres north at Ayios Sozomenos stands the shell of a Latin church that was never finished.

en: The most completely excavated medieval sugar factory in the Mediterranean, and the industrial heart of the royal estate that grew cane on the Paphos coastal plain. Marie-Louise von Wartburg dug the Stavros site in 1980 to 1982 and 1987 to 1991 and found the whole production line intact: water-driven mill, boiling house, refining floor and reservoir, running from the late thirteenth century to the end of the sixteenth. Up the slope stands the manor of Covocle, the fortified Lusignan estate house that administered it, now the site museum for Palaepaphos. The Stavros project led on to the excavation of the Hospitaller works at Kolossi and the Cornaro works at Episkopi, the three together giving Cyprus the best-known sugar archaeology anywhere.

en: A barn-roofed mountain church whose paintings were finished in 1494, given by the priest Petros Peratis and his wife Pepani and signed by Philippos Goul, a Greek-speaking painter of Syrian origin and the only named artist of late medieval Cyprus with a substantial surviving body of work. It holds the most complete fifteenth-century painted programme on the island, and its style is the thing to look at: Palaiologan formulae, local plainness and Italian Renaissance detail in the same scene, the visual signature of a Greek population under three centuries of Latin rule. Inscribed by UNESCO in 1985 as one of the painted churches of the Troodos.
